summary:
Hubert Misztela, who works at Novartis on generative AI for small molecule design, presents a framework for using LLMs in scientific discovery. The talk opens with a 1990s biology paradox: scientists overexpressing a gene in petunia flowers expected stronger color but got a color flip. Three related phenomena from different biology subdomains, each with distinct vocabulary, took eight years to connect, ultimately leading to a Nobel Prize. Misztela asks whether LLMs could accelerate such discoveries by spotting novel relationships across distant domains.

He reviews naive RAG and its enhancements (HyDE, ranking, document indexing), noting these address matching and retrieval but don't handle semantically complex questions. He emphasizes reasoning before retrieval, citing routing in agentic flows and Graph RAG. He classifies question complexity using database relationship analogies: 1:1, 1:N, and multi-concept questions spanning multiple chunks. He surveys reasoning types—Chain of Thought, logical, causal, algorithmic, probabilistic, structured, and geometric—and suggests delegating each to specialized tools.

For benchmarking, he introduces a knowledge cutoff approach: using only pre-discovery scientific papers in RAG so the LLM cannot cheat with prior knowledge of known results like RNA interference. He defines escalating success levels: finding relationships between facts, finding less obvious cross-subdomain links, exhaustive fact extraction, making new hypotheses, and ideally explaining mechanisms. He notes that even human discoverers knew what was happening but not how.

His experiments show naive RAG failed due to using post-discovery knowledge. Strict prompting improved groundedness. A relevance classifier passing all chunks through the LLM proved redundant with embedding distances. A more sophisticated prompt simulating scientist reasoning found hypotheses related to both DNA and RNA, moving in the right direction. He applies Jenks natural breaks optimization to determine how many chunks to retrieve by calculating variances within and between embedding clusters. The key finding: reasoning over the question and database before retrieval gets closer to ground truth without cheating. He concludes that scientific discovery requires harder problems than simple Q&A, knowing your problem defines more efficient RAG architecture, and brute-force LLM checking shouldn't be overlooked.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Hubert Misztela introduces himself as a Novartis researcher working on generative AI for small molecule design. He outlines the talk's structure: a biology paradox leading to a Nobel Prize, reasoning with RAG, a scientific discovery framework, and experimental examples.

sections.title: The Petunia Paradox and Nobel Prize Discovery
sections.summary: In the early 1990s, scientists overexpressing a gene in petunia flowers expected stronger color but got a color flip. Three phenomena from different biology subdomains with different names took about eight years to connect, leading to a Nobel Prize. Misztela asks whether LLMs could speed up such cross-domain discoveries.

sections.title: RAG Overview and Limitations
sections.summary: Reviews naive RAG pipeline and tricks like HyDE, ranking, and document indexing for different purposes. Highlights the core problem: if LLMs cannot handle slightly complex questions, how can they be expected to understand questions and produce correct responses through RAG.

sections.title: Reasoning Before Retrieval
sections.summary: Introduces reasoning before retrieval as a necessary step, citing routing in agentic flows and Graph RAG as approaches that process questions or data before retrieval. More semantically complex questions require more reasoning steps before retrieval.

sections.title: Chemistry Analogy and Latent Space Navigation
sections.summary: Draws analogy between RAG's reasoning-embedding-retrieval-reasoning pipeline and chemistry's latent space navigation, where embeddings are optimized for a purpose rather than simply similarity-matched. Identifies a common theme of reasoning over latent spaces.

sections.title: Question Complexity Classification
sections.summary: Classifies question complexity using database relationship analogies: 1:1 (single concept), 1:N, and multi-concept questions spanning multiple chunks. Multi-concept questions trigger the need for reasoning before retrieval to know what to retrieve.

sections.title: Types of Reasoning and Tool Delegation
sections.summary: Surveys reasoning types: Chain of Thought, logical, causal, algorithmic, probabilistic, structured, and geometric (ARC prize). Suggests delegating reasoning types to specialized tools like causal inference libraries or Python REPLs rather than expecting LLMs to handle all types well.

sections.title: Problem Setup and Groundedness
sections.summary: Defines the specific problem: process a dataset repeatedly to extract relevant themes for one critical question about the three phenomena. Emphasizes groundedness because LLMs have seen Wikipedia and know about RNA interference. Frames computational efficiency vs groundedness tradeoff and identifies relevance classifier as a key component.

sections.title: Knowledge Cutoff and Success Levels
sections.summary: Introduces knowledge cutoff methodology: using only pre-discovery scientific papers in RAG so the LLM cannot cheat. Frames this as agent training on a specific scientific problem. Defines escalating success levels: finding relationships between facts, finding less obvious cross-subdomain links, exhaustive fact extraction, making new hypotheses, and ideally explaining mechanisms—which even human discoverers initially couldn't do.

sections.title: Experiments: Naive RAG, Strict Prompting, and Relevance Classifier
sections.summary: Presents Jenks natural breaks optimization for determining how many chunks to retrieve by calculating variances within and between embedding clusters. Naive RAG failed due to using post-discovery knowledge. Strict prompting improved groundedness. Relevance classifier passing all chunks through LLM proved redundant with embedding distances. A more sophisticated prompt simulating scientist reasoning found hypotheses related to both DNA and RNA, moving in the right direction.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.summary: Concludes that scientific discovery requires solving harder problems than simple Q&A, knowing your problem defines more efficient RAG architecture, needle in haystack can be generalized, harder problems need reasoning, and brute-force LLM checking should not be overlooked as it may outperform distance embeddings.
